title: Dr. Dave
summary: Chapter 11 moves from Mangchi performances and hotel deception into bodily-health talk, Asa Akira's film work, sex-worker safety, a proposed deceptive relationship show and the long improvised ‘Dr. Dave’ session. The automated cleaner removes only six empty fragments: 2,025 raw segments become 2,019 clean segments, but the 16,167-word content is otherwise unchanged. The substantive quality layer is therefore the 299-decision human review, not a claim that the clean text is verbatim-perfect. The opening and closing Mangchi lyrics preserve alienation, violence, suicidal ideation and recovery while remaining explicitly non-quotation-grade. The studio cast is identifiable at episode level as David Choe, Asa Akira, Val/Valentin and Money Mark, with Critter discussed as absent, but zero held-out acoustic identity windows means no named line-level dialogue publishes. David describes reusing hotel rooms for sequential partners, concealing evidence and planting insects to obtain meals or upgrades; another participant describes buying and killing crickets for the same purpose. Those admissions remain in the record, while the editorial layer refuses to turn fraud, tampering or unsafe condom disposal into instructions. The room's claim that Tabasco kills germs is false: CDC food-safety guidance requires cleaning, separation, cooking and chilling, and hot sauce is not a reliable substitute. A shared warehouse blanket reportedly went unwashed through multiple sexual uses, yielding a direct sanitation conclusion rather than a reason to expose private partners or locations. The digestive-health section distinguishes first-person observations from diagnosis. David reports that a juice/smoothie-heavy Ranch diet coincided with less gas and fewer bowel movements, then blames bread and restaurant food after symptoms return. Temporal association does not establish causation, and recurrent abdominal discomfort is a healthcare signal rather than proof of an intolerance. Mayo Clinic guidance supports that intestinal gas is normal and trapped gas can cause pain or bloating; the episode does not establish the serious-harm claim attached to holding it. Airplane, yoga and sexual anecdotes remain attributed, and a private airline worker, yoga contact and sexual partners remain protected. The ant infestation follows food residue and a masturbation container left overnight; the large count is only an estimate. Asa's film is repaired from ‘Hollywood’ to *Holly... Would* (2014), directed by Brad Armstrong for Wicked Pictures, with Asa playing Holly, an escort. The room's distinction between a scripted adult feature and gonzo work is preserved without presenting budget estimates or genre claims as verified industry taxonomy. The incall/outcall discussion identifies real tradeoffs—address exposure, travel, familiarity and vulnerability—but does not operationalize weapons or expose private workers, residences, assistants or provider networks. A Mexico City massage anecdote in which a provider leaves after the client sleeps is retained with the capacity boundary that sleep cannot authorize new sexual contact. A Dubai hypothetical raises trafficking and violence risk; its dehumanizing claim about murdered migrant sex workers is not treated as evidence. Poon's delayed-orgasm story produces conflicting physical experiences and speculative explanations. Difficulty reaching orgasm does not establish sexual orientation. The proposed Colombia show would secretly pay a worker to simulate a month-long relationship and then compress extensive therapy into entertainment. Interest expressed by Poon or Asa is not final informed consent, and the worker's terms and consent are never established. The mock ‘Dr. Dave’ session repeatedly states that David is unlicensed and the format is entertainment. It nevertheless pressures Asa about what to disclose to her parents, attempts an unconsented live call, centers David's own family analogies, uses mortality to accelerate disclosure and ends in a sexualized therapist proposal. Asa supplies the essential corrections: her parents are broadly accepting, her mother periodically asks when she will stop adult work, she wants her happiness weighed against social reputation, she may withhold future retirement news partly from spite but also to retain room to change her mind, and she can hold hurt and understanding simultaneously. She rejects David's claim that she hates her mother, resists a scripted confrontation, and later asks for real therapy with a therapist who does not make the session about himself. The editorial record preserves those disagreements instead of letting the host's interpretation become diagnosis. East/West, Asian/white/Mexican and gender communication claims are speaker stereotypes, not cultural laws. Reconciliation without direct processing is one relationship example, not a universal model. A hypothetical pregnancy does not establish current pregnancy or reproductive plans. *The Sessions* (2012) is corrected as a film about Mark O'Brien and sex surrogate Cheryl Cohen-Greene, played by Helen Hunt; she is not his therapist. Television trivia repairs *Masters of Sex*, Showtime, William Masters and Virginia Johnson, Washington University in St. Louis, Beau Bridges, *Vikings*, Ragnar Lothbrok and Jax Teller. Music trivia repairs ‘I Believe’ by the stylized Blessid Union of Souls and ‘Building a Mystery’ by Sarah McLachlan, including several mangled lyric fragments verified through official artist sources. Asa explicitly refuses to amplify an idea about fans sending sexual material to parents; that boundary is honored rather than converted into searchable harassment metadata. The closing spoken school-shooting/mass-murder setup and Mangchi Peter Tong narrative retain the suicide and recovery arc without inventing exact lyrics. Nothing is censored from the source layer. The editorial layer corrects entities, marks uncertainty, protects private people and prevents unsafe, medical or therapeutic claims from masquerading as instructions or facts.

CDC food-safety guidance says to clean, separate, cook and chill; hot sauce is not a reliable substitute for safe handling: https://www.cdc.gov/food-safety/prevention/index.html

CDC's 2025 raw-oyster warning explicitly notes that hot sauce and lemon juice do not kill harmful germs: https://www.cdc.gov/media/releases/2025/2025-raw-oysters-linked-to-ongoing-salmonella-outbreak-almost-half-of-u-s-states-reporting-cases.html

Mayo Clinic says intestinal gas is a normal digestive byproduct and trapped gas can cause pain or bloating; that does not validate the episode's broad serious-harm claim: https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/gas-and-gas-pains/symptoms-causes/syc-20372709
IMDb credits *Holly... Would* (2014), Brad Armstrong and Asa Akira as Holly: https://www.imdb.com/title/tt4412316/fullcredits/

XBIZ independently places *Holly...Would* in Asa Akira and Brad Armstrong's Wicked Pictures award context: https://www.xbiz.com/news/187964/wicked-pictures-receives-75-nominations-for-2015-xbiz-awards

IMDb and a contemporary CBS interview ground *The Sessions* and Helen Hunt's sex-surrogate role: https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1866249/ and https://www.cbsnews.com/news/helen-hunt-says-she-hadnt-heard-of-a-sex-surrogate-until-the-sessions/
Sarah McLachlan's official song page verifies *Building a Mystery*: https://www.sarahmclachlan.com/track/building-a-mystery/

Apple Music verifies the stylized artist name Blessid Union of Souls, and Shazam provides the *I Believe* lyric reference: https://music.apple.com/us/artist/blessid-union-of-souls/639950 and https://www.shazam.com/song/724410986/i-believe?tab=lyrics

The opening/closing Mangchi lyrics, Peter Tong/Tom variants, the exact keyboard model, several private names and some trivia answers remain audio/video-verification candidates rather than silent repairs.
